title: Wrong Patient
passages:
Ospina didn't wait to be asked. They dropped the hopper—a yard mule's big, dumb cousin, a low steel tray on six tires built to haul ballast and nothing cleverer—into gear and swung it broadside into the gap, filling it like a cork in a bottle.

The feral rig's nose sensor was still reading the world off the last good picture it had before the Blank swallowed its signal, and that picture now had four tons of parked hopper where open road used to be. It stopped dead, ten centimeters off the steel, brake lights on and staying on. It would sit there trusting a world that no longer existed until somebody handed it a new heading, and nobody was going to.

"Nice parking," Rhea said.

"I seal rigs, I don't park them," Ospina said. "Get your box up."

The mule coughed when Rhea keyed it. She'd pulled its drive relay and smashed the cab panel to kill the lockout, so she had steering back, but she had to hold the throttle wire against the post with her thumb, and the whole rig moved like a thing that resented being awake. The tow bar sat down at the lip of the culvert, the box tail hanging over the pipe, the sedated man rolling loose inside. She fed it power in threads, a few centimeters at a time, feeling for the moment the weight came off the tail and onto the road.

"Easy," Miko said, both palms flat on the box's rear doors like she could hold it up by wanting to. "Easy, easy—"

The tail came up. The tires bit gravel. All of it on solid ground now, mule and box and the man who wasn't on any manifest anyone would read.

Rhea took her thumb off the wire and the mule died again, and she sat there breathing.

Ospina was already turning the hopper's wheel, backing it out of the gap, and the moment it moved the feral rig crept forward half a meter and stopped behind the mule, obedient to a heading only it could see.

"Come with us," Rhea said. "We're blind out here. No transponder, no nav, no board. You've got the chipped stamp, you've got—"

"I've got a shift ending at oh-six-hundred and a door that reads my badge every time I walk through it." Ospina held up the stamp, the one with the corner chipped out, and Rhea saw for the first time that it wasn't Ospina's hand that had done the resealing—Ospina held it the way you hold something you found. "This plate your loader jammed in the track." They tipped their head at the hinge still wedged in the door. "Not Bay 4 stock. I sign out every plate we run and I never signed that one out. Somebody walked it into my yard tonight, and it wasn't me."

"Then help me—"

"Then I've got a long dark between me and a clean board, and if I'm not standing at that door at six, the next thing I seal is my own cell." Ospina swung the hopper around, pointed it back toward Kettering, toward whatever waited there with a chipped stamp and a manifest built out of lies. "Forty klicks to Anza. You did thirty before you met me. Do the rest."

And they were gone, taillights shrinking into the Blank.

Miko looked at Rhea. Rhea looked east.

"Forty klicks," she said. "Blind. In a rig that can't shout its own number." Somewhere past the end of that road Ivo was under a cracked diaphragm, breathing for both of them on borrowed parts, and every one of these kilometers was one he didn't have.

She thumbed the wire. The mule woke up angry.

"Then let's not tell it its number," Miko said, climbing into the passenger side. "Let's just drive."

Rhea drove. Dead signal, a box that logged no one, and a passenger she trusted less than the truck—and at the far end, her brother counting down every kilometer she hadn't covered yet.

The Blank ran east in a shallow trough of old riverbed, and the mule took it at forty because Rhea wouldn't give it more. Over forty the washboard shook the throttle wire out from under her thumb, and then they were cargo like the box behind them.

Miko rode with her boots on the dash and the repeater turned toward her—the pod's own four-line screen, copied forward on a wire so the driver can read it without climbing out into the weather.

"Passenger core temperature stable," she said. "Thirty-six point four."

"Good."

"Thirty-six point four."

"I heard you the first time."

"It's been thirty-six point four since Kettering." Miko tapped the glass. "It's a nice number. I'd like a different one."

Rhea kept her thumb down and thought about it, because a man under sedation does not hold a number. The heater cycles, the pump in the mattress pad kicks, the box breathes: thirty-six two, thirty-six six, thirty-six three. She'd sat with a hundred of these screens on rigs she had no business touching.

She also knew what the box did when its databus died—the cable bundle that carries the sensor readings up to the screen. It didn't blank. It held the last page it had read. Last good picture. Same as the feral rig back there, stopped dead on a road that had moved.

There was a clamp meter in the door pocket, tongs that close around a cable and read the current running through it without cutting anything. She leaned, clamped it on the pod's cell lead, and watched the digits settle.

One point two amps. A sedated hundred-kilo man, a heater, and a mattress pump should have been pulling five or six.

She put her palm over the box's exhaust vent and held it there long enough to be sure. Cold. No heat coming out of a box that was supposedly holding a man at thirty-six point four.

"See," Miko said. "Dead."

"Cold isn't dead." Rhea dropped the meter back in the pocket. "The box is dead. That's a different problem."

"Is it? Because from in here they look like the same problem with better manners."

Ahead, low on the horizon, the sky had a stain on it: sodium light, Anza's main gate, where the reader shouts every rig's number out to the board and the board writes it down. Except this rig had no transponder to shout with, which meant it would arrive as nothing at all, and a nothing at a gate is worse than a number.

"Left at the leaning post," Miko said.

Rhea took the left. Two hundred meters on, Miko said, "Right. Slow."

"There's no road here."

"There's a siding." Miko pointed with two fingers, like she was calling a card. "Freight spur. Ore hoppers loaded there back when anybody shipped ore. The gate never reads it because there's nothing on it to read."

Rhea pulled the wire up a thread and let the mule roll, and looked at her. "You've driven this."

"I've never driven anything in my life. I load it."

"Then how do you know where the ore siding is."

Miko was quiet for three posts. Then she said, "Because I've been walking it since Kettering. Not this stretch, the maps of it. I counted the reflectors off a hopper seat on a night shift nobody was watching, and I know there's a stub of dead road in the dark on the east side of Anza, and I know what leaves from it at oh-four-hundred." She shrugged. "Three tickets to the coast, three names, all paid. If I roll through that lit gate tonight I'm a body on a board, and the exit I bought burns with me."

"You could have said that in the yard."

"You'd have put me off the mule."

"I still might."

"You won't. You need somebody who knows where the dark is." Miko grinned at her, entirely too pleased. "Also I'm fun."

Rhea did the arithmetic she'd been doing for an hour, the only arithmetic that mattered: forty klicks at forty, and an hour of Ivo breathing through a cracked diaphragm at the far end of it, waiting on a sister who was driving a truck with her thumb.

The siding came up on the right, black gravel, no light on any of it.

She took her thumb off the wire and the mule died, and in the quiet she climbed down and walked back along the box with the meter still in her fist. Thirty-six point four, on a screen that hadn't read the man once all night.

She put her hand flat on the pod lid.

It was warm. Not machine-warm. Warm like a person.

The lid was warm under her palm, and the mule was dead, and for a couple of seconds Rhea stood in the dark with her hand on a man she'd spent forty kilometers believing was a number on a screen.

Then the yard light came on.

One sodium lamp on a bent pole at the end of the stub, buzzing up from nothing to orange, and under it a man in a relay operator's coveralls with a hand lamp—a rubber torch you carry when the mast lights are out and you don't trust your own feet.

"Kill that," Rhea said.

He killed it. Then he came on anyway, unhurried, the way a man walks when the ground is his.

"You're on Anza ore siding," he said. "I'm Teodoro, I run the relay here, and I've been on the board since twenty-two hundred, which means I know things. Anza didn't file a medical handoff tonight. Not one. A handoff is the other end saying *send him, I'm ready, I've got the bay warm*—and nobody said it. No inbound medical, no outbound, no pod, nothing." He rapped the box's flank with his knuckles. "This isn't on my board. It isn't on any board. It's a Kettering ghost with a Kettering yard on the side of it, and nobody in this node is expecting a patient."

"There's a man in it," Rhea said.

"There's a man in a lot of things. There's a coast hopper string comes through this stub at oh-four-hundred, for instance, and I don't know why I said that."

"Don't," Miko said, from the far side of the mule, where she had arranged herself into a shape that was mostly shadow.

"Don't what?"

"Don't *finish* anything. You're a talker. I've met talkers."

Rhea took her hand off the lid and put it back on, because the warmth was the only reading tonight that hadn't lied to her. "The pod screen says thirty-six point four, steady, all the way from Kettering."

"Which screen?"

"The repeater. On a wire, off the pod."

Teodoro made a small noise, the kind you make at a child carrying a full cup. "Databus is cut, or that screen would be arguing with itself. Last good page. It'll hold thirty-six point four till the sun comes up." He tipped the lamp toward the box's belly without switching it on. "What's the cell pulling?"

"One point two amps."

"Then it's cold and it's holding a picture of a warm man." He scratched his jaw. "Also your brother's in my shop on the yard bottle, and I taped his diaphragm, and it holds as long as he doesn't argue with it. Four hours of bottle. Maybe five if I turn the shop heater down, which I have."

Rhea stood very still with her thumb near the throttle wire. "You could have led with that."

"You could have led with why you're parked on my siding with a rig that can't shout its own number." He said it without heat, and then he laughed once. "Ah. There it is. Never mind, I don't want it."

"I want to know who's in the box."

"Everybody wants to know that. It's the only interesting question on this continent tonight." He came around to the rear doors and crouched, and ran two fingers under the lip of the lid where the seal sat in its channel—Bay 4 stock, four bolts, a chipped stamp's ghost still visible in the wax. "Pod's got a manual release here. Under the lip. You pull it, the lid comes up on the strut, and the pod logs an open."

"Logs it to who? It's got no databus."

"To nobody. That's the mercy of it." He looked up. "But it breaks the seal. Once it's open it's never sealed again, and I've spent eleven years in this yard learning not to break a seal I can't re-stamp. I don't have a stamp. I don't have a plate. I've got a hole in my stock I can't explain to a man at oh-six-hundred."

"Then don't touch it," Rhea said. "I'll touch it."

She got her fingers under the lip. The wax was soft. It had been warm for a while.

From inside the box, three times, something knocked.

PASSAGE ends.
